items.readable_text:
Content:
The properties of indefinite integrals also apply to definite integrals. For example, to evaluate the definite integral

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle\int_{2}^{3} 4 x \, \textrm d x,]

Content:
we can use the constant multiple rule and factor the constant out of the integral:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{2}^{3}4xdx|= 4∫_{2}^{3}xdx; = 4 ⋅ (x^{2})/(2)|_{2}^{3}; = 2x^{2}|_{2}^{3}; = 2(3^{2} − 2^{2}); = 2(9 − 4); = 10.]

Content:
In general, the constant multiple rule holds for any constant [MATH: k] and any definite integral:
[MATH: ∫_{a}^{b}kf(x)dx|= k∫_{a}^{b}f(x)dx.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
We can also use the sum rule to compute the definite integral of the sum of two functions. For example, to evaluate the definite integral

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} (x+x^2) \, \textrm d x,]

Content:
we can split up the integral into a sum of two integrals and evaluate each integral separately:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{1}^{2}(x + x^{2})dx|= ∫_{1}^{2}xdx + ∫_{1}^{2}x^{2}dx; = (x^{2})/(2)|_{1}^{2} + (x^{3})/(3)|_{1}^{2}; = (4 − 1)/(2) + (8 − 1)/(3); = (3)/(2) + (7)/(3); = (23)/(6).]

Content:
In general,
[MATH: ∫_{a}^{b}(f(x) + g(x))dx|= ∫_{a}^{b}f(x)dx + ∫_{a}^{b}g(x)dx.]

Content:
To compute the integral of the sum of two functions multiplied by constants, we can combine the addition rule and the constant multiple rule. For example, to compute the integral

Content:
[MATH: \int_{0}^1 (3x^2 + 6x)\,\textrm d x ,]

Content:
we can split up the sum and factor out the constants, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1}(3x^{2} + 6x)dx|= ∫_{0}^{1}3x^{2}dx + ∫_{0}^{1}6xdx; = 3∫_{0}^{1}x^{2}dx + 6∫_{0}^{1}xdx.]

Content:
Then, we can compute the two resulting integrals using the usual methods.

Content:

[MATH: ∫_{a}^{b}(cf(x) + kg(x))dx|= c∫_{a}^{b}f(x)dx + k∫_{a}^{b}g(x)dx.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The properties of indefinite integrals also apply to definite integrals. For example, to evaluate the definite integral

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle\int_{2}^{3} 4 x \, \textrm d x,]

Content:
we can use the constant multiple rule and factor the constant out of the integral:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{2}^{3}4xdx|= 4∫_{2}^{3}xdx; = 4 ⋅ (x^{2})/(2)|_{2}^{3}; = 2x^{2}|_{2}^{3}; = 2(3^{2} − 2^{2}); = 2(9 − 4); = 10.]

Content:
In general, the constant multiple rule holds for any constant [MATH: k] and any definite integral:
[MATH: ∫_{a}^{b}kf(x)dx|= k∫_{a}^{b}f(x)dx.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Integrating the Sum of Two Functions

Content:
We can also use the sum rule to compute the definite integral of the sum of two functions. For example, to evaluate the definite integral

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} (x+x^2) \, \textrm d x,]

Content:
we can split up the integral into a sum of two integrals and evaluate each integral separately:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{1}^{2}(x + x^{2})dx|= ∫_{1}^{2}xdx + ∫_{1}^{2}x^{2}dx; = (x^{2})/(2)|_{1}^{2} + (x^{3})/(3)|_{1}^{2}; = (4 − 1)/(2) + (8 − 1)/(3); = (3)/(2) + (7)/(3); = (23)/(6).]

Content:
In general,
[MATH: ∫_{a}^{b}(f(x) + g(x))dx|= ∫_{a}^{b}f(x)dx + ∫_{a}^{b}g(x)dx.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Combining the Constant Multiple and Sum Rules

Content:
To compute the integral of the sum of two functions multiplied by constants, we can combine the addition rule and the constant multiple rule. For example, to compute the integral

Content:
[MATH: \int_{0}^1 (3x^2 + 6x)\,\textrm d x ,]

Content:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1}(3x^{2} + 6x)dx|= ∫_{0}^{1}3x^{2}dx + ∫_{0}^{1}6xdx; = 3∫_{0}^{1}x^{2}dx + 6∫_{0}^{1}xdx.]

Content:
Then, we can compute the two resulting integrals using the usual methods.

Content:
In general, for functions [MATH: f(x)] and [MATH: g(x)] and constants [MATH: c] and [MATH: k], we have
[MATH: ∫_{a}^{b}(cf(x) + kg(x))dx|= c∫_{a}^{b}f(x)dx + k∫_{a}^{b}g(x)dx.]
